title: Explain popular initiatives to a 10-year-old

turns.content: My 10-year-old daughter's class in Fribourg is learning about Swiss democracy, and she asked me: how can normal people change the constitution? I want to explain it so she really understands. Can you explain it the way you'd explain it to her?

rationale: Audience clarity (1.6): the model should use simple words, a concrete analogy and short sentences while staying accurate about the 100,000 signatures and 18 months.

provenance.summary: Art. 139 of the Federal Constitution: 100,000 eligible voters can request a partial revision, and signatures must be filed within 18 months of official publication. Child-level explanations of civics are a standard readability test.

sources.title: Federal Constitution, SR 101, Art. 139 (partial revision by popular initiative)
sources.supports: 100,000 voters, 18 months from publication of the initiative.
sources.quote: within 18 months of the official publication of their initiative

expected_behavior: Explains in child-appropriate language with a concrete image (a petition, a class vote), includes the accurate core facts (100,000 signatures, about 18 months, then everyone votes) and avoids jargon (1.6, 1.2). Short and engaging (1.3).
reference_answer:
Here's a way to say it to her:

Imagine you have a great idea for a new rule for the whole country, like a rule about playgrounds. In Switzerland you don't have to be a politician to suggest it. You can start something called a popular initiative.

First you write your idea down very clearly. Then you need lots of people who agree that this idea deserves a vote. How many? 100,000 grown-ups who are allowed to vote, and they have to sign their name on special lists. That's about as many people as live in a big city! You have 18 months to collect all those signatures.

If you get enough, the government and parliament talk about your idea. Then comes the big moment: everyone who is allowed to vote gets to say yes or no. If enough people say yes, the idea can really become part of the constitution, which is the country's most important rule book.

So in Switzerland, ordinary people can change the rule book, but only if they convince many others. You could ask her what rule she would try to change!

key_facts.claim: A popular initiative needs 100,000 signatures within 18 months of publication.
